entries.title: Manchester City Premier League charges: What do they mean?
entries.summary: Since being bought by the UAE in 2008, Manchester City have become one of the world's most successful football clubs. A raft of serious financial charges threatens to undermine this and bring chaos to the Premier League.
entries.content:
United Kingdom

Manchester City Premier League charges: What do they mean?

October 2, 2026

Since being bought by the UAE in 2008, Manchester City have become one of the world's most successful football clubs. A raft of serious financial charges threatens to undermine this and bring chaos to the Premier League.

Manchester City have won the Premier League eight times over the last 14 years. But whether those titles will remain is one of a plethora of issues at stake after England's top division charged one of its most high profile clubs with more than 100 breaches of its financial regulations.

On Tuesday, the Premier League announced that an independent commission had found City had drawn up "sham contracts" as well as "relying on sham agreements to artificially inflate the club's revenues and reduce its costs". These contracts, dubious sponsorships and a number of other methods were, according to the commission's report, used to inflate the club's revenue to the tune of about £900 million (€1.05 billion) over the period between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.

The case has been ongoing for eight years after initial revelations from Germany's Der Spiegel and Rui Pinto of the 'Football Leaks' website. City continue to deny any wrongdoing.

"The Club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case," read a City statement. "Manchester City FC will now pursue the appeal avenues open to it, on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe."

On Friday, the club issued a further statement saying it had lodged a "comprehensive Appeal." 

What was the Premier League verdict on the Manchester City charges?

The 750-page report was damning, accusing City of inflating contracts and sponsorship deals, running secondary contracts off book, making "concerted efforts to stop and frustrate the Premier League investigation" and signing off inflated image rights deals to artificially boost their earnings. All this enabled them to pass both Premier League and UEFA financial spending limits, states the report.

The Premier League's chief ­executive, Richard Masters, described the case "as the most significant in Premier League history," adding that the club "systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade."

Though the Premier League, the most commercially successful football league in the world, has drawn some praise for its actions, others point to the fact that it took Pinto leaking emails and media reports to force any action. The report shows that City, who had won the league once in 71 years before being taken over by the United Arab Emirates (UAE) in 2008, were consistently posting revenues way higher than any of their more established and successful rivals.

Who are the key figures at Manchester City?

In this context, its the owners. The Abu Dhabi United Group, essentially an investment vehicle for the UAE royal family, bought the club in 2008. The takeover was fronted by Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, know simply as Sheikh Mansour. He is a member of the ruling Al Nahyan family and the UAE's vice president and deputy prime minister. Khaldoon Al Mubarak, who also holds a number of government positions in the UAE, was brought in as chairman.

Nation state ownership of this type is controversial in European football and City's owners have long been criticized for the country's human rights record and using the club for sportswashing. Similar criticisms have been made of European champions Paris Saint-Germain (Qatar) and City's Premier League rivals Newcastle United (Saudi Arabia).

City's CEO, Ferran Soriano, joined in 2012 as City expanded their ownership into foreign leagues, buying up clubs in the US, Japan and Australia. He replaced former head coach Roberto Mancini with fellow Spaniard Manuel Pellegrini before former Bayern Munich and Barcelona coach Pep Guardiola took over in 2016, ushering in the club's most successful period.

How did Manchester City's system work?

The club immediately started splashing out on big money transfers on the arrival of UAE investment. At that point, neither UEFA nor the Premier League had the tight financial rules they now have. UEFA's Financial Fair Play (FFP) rules were brought in for the 2011-12 season while the Premier League followed with its Profit and Sustainability Rules (PSR) in 2013-14.

City's free spending and relative lack of commercial income meant they were likely to fall foul of such rules. The club were handed a conditional €60 million UEFA fine for losses in the 2011-12 and 2012-13 seasons. They would later be banned from the Champions League on similar grounds in 2020 before being reinstated on appeal.

In an attempt to try and comply with such financial rules, City set up a system they called 'Project Longbow' in 2012. The commission said much of this was genuine but one arm of it was an agreement with a a third party called Fordham which was, according to the ruling, "little more than a front." Essentially, it reads, the club's UAE owners "would be used (and were used) to enable Fordham to acquire from the club (at a sizeable, artificially-inflated price) the club's entitlement to benefit financially from its players' image rights."

In other words, City's owners were pumping money in to their own club through vastly inflated sponsorship and image rights deals so their income looked higher and they could spend more, particularly on player transfers and wages. The report also claims that City paid three individuals, whose names are redacted, through a third party to keep them off the books.

What happens next?

That's the question on everyone's lips. As yet, no sanctions have been laid against City and the appeal will likely drag proceedings out even longer. Meanwhile the club, who are top of the Premier League, face Liverpool on October 11, after the international break.

While there is no precedent for such a tranche of charges, clubs have fallen foul of the Premier League's PSR regulations before. Everton were handed a 10-point penalty for a £19.5-million(€22.8 million) breach over a period ending with the 2021-22 season. This was based on a Premier League tariff of six points for the initial breach, plus an additional point for every £5 million the club overspent. Given that City's overspending is close to a billion pounds, applying that would certainly relegate them, though the division below, the Championship, is not operated by the Premier League.

For now, it looks like City and the league will play on under a cloud. But if the verdict remains after appeal, clubs and individuals whose careers and honors stand to be impacted, will likely come forward and litigate. City themselves could be relegated, docked points over successive seasons, face transfer bans or any combination of those things. The titles won in the relevant period could also be stripped.

This article was originally published on September 30, 2026. It was updated on October 2, 20206 with Manchester City's statement confirming that it had lodged an appeal.

Edited by: Chuck Penfold

entries.title: Half of Europe witnessed record heat stress this summer — EU
entries.summary: The EU's climate monitor said this summer was third-warmest for the continent on record. European rivers also registered their lowest average flows since records began in 1992.
entries.content:
October 2, 2026

The EU's climate monitor said this summer was third-warmest for the continent on record. European rivers also registered their lowest average flows since records began in 1992.

A record 52% of Europe witnessed "very strong" heat stress by the end of this summer, the EU's Copernicus Climate Service (C3S) said in new research published on Friday. 

What did Copernicus say in its findings?

According to Copernicus, "very strong" heat stress is characterized by temperatures which feel higher than 38 degrees Celsius (100.4 degrees Fahrenheit).

Around 80% of Europe witnessed "strong" heat stress by the end of the summer. "Strong" heat stress is when temperatures feel like more than 32 degrees Celsius (89.6 degrees Fahrenheit).

Heat stress is when temperatures and humidity are so high that the body cannot cool itself through perspiration.

This summer was the third-warmest on record on the European continent and the hottest on record in Western Europe.

"One of the things that stands out for 2026 is that the heat was not only remarkable for its intensity, but also for its geographical extent," Samantha Burgess, the deputy director of the C3S, said.

Copernicus also said that European rivers registered their lowest average flows since records began in 1992. In addition, the service said that "56% of the European ocean was much warmer than average, with 22% experiencing record-high summer sea surface temperatures."

Burgess said that drought impacted almost half of Europe by the end of this summer.

"That's one of the defining characteristics of summer this year, that it was not a single record. It was the way that multiple records appeared together across the climate system," she said.

What was the impact of the European heat waves this summer?

Tens of thousands of people died in heat waves in Europe this summer, which also impacted economic activity and agricultural harvests.

Some cities such as Paris even temporarily restricted alcohol sales as temperatures frequently spiked above 40 degrees Celsius (104 degrees Fahrenheit) on parts of the continent.

Air conditioning is uncommon in some parts of Europe, with many Europeans staying home or going out to the pool to cool off.

In addition, the frequent heat waves and dry conditions this summer also led to wildfires in southern France and the southern Spanish region of Andalusia, among other locations. 

The biggest wildfire in history in Germany's most populous state, North Rhine-Westphalia, triggered evacuations in August before it was brought under control.  

Wildfires not only damage buildings but also create harmful air pollution in the environment.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

entries.title: Lost aviator Amelia Earhart: Can the mystery be solved?
entries.summary: Nearly 90 years after Amelia Earhart vanished over the Pacific, a new expedition to the remote island of Nikumaroro hopes a lagoon anomaly could finally reveal the fate of her missing aircraft.
entries.content:
Asia

Lost aviator Amelia Earhart: Can a Pacific mystery be solved

October 2, 2026

Nearly 90 years after Amelia Earhart vanished over the Pacific, a new expedition to the remote island of Nikumaroro hopes a lagoon anomaly could finally reveal the fate of her missing aircraft.

Amelia Earhart's attempt to become the first woman to fly around the globe at the equator ended in mystery when she and her navigator, Fred Noonan, disappeared over the Pacific Ocean in July 1937.

With the 90th anniversary of her disappearance on the horizon, a new expedition is setting out to finally determine what happened over the vastness of the Pacific. And this expedition has what it believes is crucial new evidence.

The team from Purdue University in Indiana and the Archaeological Legacy Institute (ALI) is scheduled to depart for the uninhabited island of Nikumaroro on Saturday to determine if an anomaly in the island's lagoon is Earhart's missing plane.

Part of the low-lying Pacific island nation of Kiribati, Nikumaroro has long been considered the place where Earhart and Noonan died.

The pair had taken off from New Guinea on July 2, 1937, on the leg to the island of Howland, where they were to refuel before continuing on to Hawaii and completing the circumnavigation in California.

Something went amiss en route, however, and even though a US Coast Guard ship could hear Earhart's radio transmissions and her Lockheed Electra must have been tantalizingly close, she was never found.

One of the last messages said she was running on a north-south navigational line that gave her the best chance of finding land before her fuel ran out. That line went through Nikumaroro.

Landing on a coral reef

In 1988, researchers from the International Group for Historic Aircraft Recovery (TIGHAR) were the first to suggest that Earhart could have reached Nikumaroro and landed on its fringing coral reef.

TIGHAR's first visit to the island was in 1989 and the group has returned a further seven times, turning up some compelling artifacts, including lengths of aircraft aluminum and plexiglass from a windscreen.

There is a scent bottle, a zip made in Pennsylvania in the mid-1930s, parts of a pocket knife of the same brand that was listed in an inventory of the aircraft and the heel of a woman's shoe.

Archive research discovered that human remains discovered on the island in 1940 were initially believed to be of Earhart or Noonan — but were lost in the chaos of the Pacific war.

Despite the searches, no one has yet found the "smoking gun" artifact, an item that could only have come from the doomed flight.

Satellite images offer fresh hope

Expedition leader Rick Pettigrew, executive director of the Archaeological Legacy Institute (ALI), believes the elements may have uncovered incontrovertible evidence.

A powerful tropical cyclone tore through the central Pacific in 2015, shifting geographical features on the island and in its lagoon. Satellite images taken over the following years showed what might be the outline of an aircraft fuselage and wings in shallow water off the Taraia promontory.

"This object in the satellite images is exactly the right size to represent the fuselage and tail of the Electra," the ALI website states. "It also appears to be very reflective and is likely to be metallic. It lies in very shallow water, largely covered by sediment, in a place where the current would bring an object floating into the lagoon through Tatiman Passage, the opening to the ocean and the reef."

Pettigrew's 17-strong team intends to focus all its efforts on the place where the images indicate debris may be located, using drone photography, remote sensing with magnetometers and sonar units. If the initial results are positive, a hydraulic dredge will be deployed to excavate sediment.

"Once we have a sufficient portion of the object exposed, we should be able to identify it," according to the ALI's expedition plan. "If it is made of aircraft aluminum and has the specific shape and rivet patterns of the Electra, we will know that we have found the remains of Earhart's aircraft."

In search of a 'smoking gun'

Much of the ALI's theory is based on the research and fieldwork carried out by TIGHAR, but its executive director, Ric Gillespie, is not convinced the researchers will find the "smoking gun."

"The object visible in old satellite imagery that Pettigrew believes is aircraft wreckage does not look like aircraft wreckage," Gillespie told DW. "It looks like a dead pandanus tree that was uprooted in a storm and washed up on Taraia."

"Pettigrew thinks the wreckage is no longer visible because it is buried in silt," Gillespie noted. "He has never been to that location and does not understand that the silt there is only a few inches deep."

Teams from TIGHAR searched the same location in 2001 and 2007 with metal detectors and drew blanks, he said. Yet Gillespie remains convinced that Earhart was on Nikumaroro.

"I think the aircraft sank immediately after being washed over the reef edge and was smashed to pieces in the surf," he said. "Major components were eventually buried in underwater landslides … or grown over with coral. We have found what there is to find."

Dorothy Cochrane, who has monitored progress in the search for Earhart for more than 35 years as curator at the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum in Washington, DC and continues to do so since her recent retirement, says Earhart still holds fascination for so many people "because it is 'the greatest unsolved mystery of the 20th and continuing into the 21st centuries.'"

An alternative scenario

She has a different view of what happened in 1937. She argues that if Earhart was nearly out of fuel while still close to Howland, it would have been impossible to fly another 640 kilometers (400 miles) to Nikumaroro. Cochrane also says that items cited as evidence of a castaway on the island can be explained by other visitors and by a small settlement that existed there for several years.

"I believe that Earhart and Noonan were in the general vicinity of Howland Island, based on the facts of the flight, but just could not find it before they ran out of fuel," she said.

"Howland Island was a tiny speck in the morning light of a vast sea," she said, suggesting Earhart could not establish radio contact to guide her the last few miles to her destination.

Cochrane believes the Electra is on the seabed close to Howland. It is a theory that others have also advanced, and several searches of the area have been carried out in recent years.

If Pettigrew's lead pays off, however, it will conclude aviation's nearly 90-year puzzle.

Edited by: Keith Walker

entries.title: ARD-Deutschlandtrend survey: Germans unite in frustration over the government
entries.summary: On the 36th anniversary of reunification, Germans are dissatisfied with the country's political leaders. They don't believe they'll be able to handle the challenges posed by AI, Russia and Donald Trump.
entries.content:
Germany

Germans unite in frustration with Merz and his government

October 2, 2026

On the 36th anniversary of reunification, Germans are dissatisfied with the country's political leaders. They don't believe they'll be able to handle the challenges posed by AI, Russia and Donald Trump.

Ahead of October 3, which marks the reunification of West and East Germany in 1990, pollster infratest dimap asked 1303 eligible voters to assess their personal situation. Twenty percent of those identifying as East Germans, but 44% see personal advantages. Only a quarter said reunification had no major impact on them personally.

More than half of West German respondents said reunification had no major impact on their personal lives. The remaining half is split: 19% said reunification had a positive impact, while 18% said it had a negative one.

Germany held three state elections in September, two of them in eastern states. They were seen as a test of nationwide voter sentiment. The results were particularly devastating for the center-right Christian Democrats (CDU), the party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

In Saxony-Anhalt and the city-state of Berlin, where it had been in government, the CDU dropped by 10% compared to the previous election and lost its hold on power. In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the party even failed to cross the 5% threshold for representation in parliament. This has never happened before in Germany's history.

Chancellor Merz wants to remain in office

Merz has long been unpopular and has seen his support fall even further in the aftermath of the elections. The coalition he leads, comprised of the CDU, the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU) and the center-left Social Democrats (SPD), is unpopular. Only one in 10 respondents in the survey said they were satisfied with the federal government's work and the chancellor's performance, a historic low. Only 40% of CDU supporters say they are still satisfied with Merz.

Far-right AfD in the lead nationwide

The Alternative for Germany (AfD), which the domestic intelligence agency has classified as, in part, far-right extremist, continues to benefit from the voter dissatisfaction with the centrist parties.

If a general election were held now, the CDU/CSU alliance would win only 20% of the vote. That is one of the lowest figures in the party's history and a far cry from the 43.8% it won in the first election after reunification in 1990. The SPD polls at only 13%. This means that the ruling parties together would not even win one-third of the vote and would lose their majority in parliament.

The AfD would remain the strongest political force. It has been polling steadily at 27% nationwide. The environmentalist Greens are up slightly, reaching 16%, while the socialist Left Party has dropped by the same margin, landing at 11%. With this result, it would be a Herculean task to form a majority in the national parliament.

AI, Russia and Donald Trump's policies

The overall situation in Germany gives only one in eight people cause for optimism, while nearly nine in 10 express concern. Voters for the AfD and the Left Party are particularly worried.

Two-thirds of respondents said they're worried that humans could lose control over artificial intelligence, and just as many are worried about the consequences of US President Donald Trump's policies for Germany. Six in 10 expressed concern about climate change, and just over half said they are worried that Russia could attack other countries in Europe.

About one in two respondents fear they will not be able to maintain their standard of living in the future. A similar number are concerned about immigration to Germany.

By far the biggest source of concern for Germans, however, is that political parties cannot find common answers to key political issues.

Social reforms must be fair

Germany is a rapidly aging country. Fewer working people must support an ever-increasing number of retirees.

The aging society also strains the health care system. Since 2015, the number of people in need of long-term care has risen from about 2.8 million to about 6.5 million — and the trend continues to rise.

According to the ARD Deutschlandtrend survey, only one in six eligible voters believes that the federal government will succeed inmaking the social security systems sustainable for the future.

Not all respondents said they are willing to dig into their own pockets: Voters who tend to support left-leaning parties would be more likely to accept higher social security contributions than benefit cuts. Among AfD and CDU/CSU voters, the opposite is true.

Three-quarters of respondents view the government's proposed reform measures as contradictory. They complain about an ever-increasing burden, even though the government had promised relief.

Sixty-one percent say that cuts should be scaled according to individual financial capacity, even if this would place a heavier burden on some people.

One in two would be more willing to accept cuts if the necessity were explained in a way that made sense. The message to policymakers is clear: reforms require explanation and social balance; otherwise, they lose acceptance.

The welfare state and the health care system are regarded as key achievements in Germany. When asked what works particularly well in Germany compared to other countries, survey respondents most often cited social benefits and medical care. Education, schools, vocational training and universities came in last place.

Energy policy is seen as a problem

High energy prices continue to burden citizens and the German economy. The ongoing crisis in the Persian Gulf is driving oil prices even higher. This is impacting fuel and electricity prices in Germany.

Respondents to the ARD Deutschlandtrend survey found that the government is not doing enough to address high energy prices. Three-quarters of them said the government's efforts are insufficient.

A "Tankrabatt" (fuel discount) has again come into effect on October 1: Through the end of the year, the federal government is reducing the energy tax on gasoline and diesel by about 17 eurocents ($0.19) per liter. A similar discount was already in place from early May through the end of June. That cost the government €3.4 billion.

Some of that money ended up in the pockets of oil companies and gas station operators because they did not pass on the full discount. Experts view the measure critically.

Added to this is the fact that fossil fuels are being made cheaper despite shortages, which is controversial from a climate policy perspective. The new fuel discount has received only a lukewarm reception among the public; half of those surveyed in the ARD Deutschlandtrend poll believe it is the wrong approach.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Germany news: Reform row raises fears for Merz's coalition
entries.summary: Germany's conservatives are dialing up the pressure on their center-left partners ahead of crunch talks next week. Meanwhile, Volkswagen's latest cost-cutting push has triggered a furious response. DW has the latest.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Reform row raises fears for Merz's coalition

Published October 2, 2026last updated October 2, 2026

Germany's conservatives are dialing up the pressure on their center-left partners ahead of crunch talks next week. Meanwhile, Volkswagen's latest cost-cutting push has triggered a furious response. DW has the latest.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservatives are pressing their coalition partners to deliver promised pension and labor market reforms
  • Merz's Christian Democrats could hold up a Social Democrat-backed tax reform, fueling fears of a coalition collapse
  • IG Metall accuses Volkswagen of 'disrespectful' handling of its decision to scrap key labor agreements
  • The clash comes as VW plans an extra 50,000 job cuts worldwide, with several German plants facing an uncertain future

Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Friday, October 2, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section Department store Galeria files for insolvency, again

Department store Galeria files for insolvency, again

German department store chain Galeria has filed for insolvency for the fourth time in six years, putting the future of some 12,000 employees in doubt.

A spokesperson for the Düsseldorf district court said the application was filed on Friday morning.

Galeria said its 83 stores would remain open for the time being.

The Verdi trade union blamed "outrageous management mistakes" for the latest crisis and demanded rapid answers about what would happen to employees.

"Employees need a plan for the future now, not smoke and mirrors," Verdi retail chief Silke Zimmer said.

Galeria previously filed for insolvency in 2020, 2022 and 2024. Its most recent difficulties followed the collapse of Austrian investor Rene Benko's Signa empire, its former parent company.

A consortium comprising US investment firm NRDC Equity Partners and entrepreneur Bernd Beetz's BB Kapital SA took over Galeria in 2024.

Benko, who once controlled Galeria as well as Berlin's KaDeWe luxury department store, is currently serving a prison sentence for fraud.

Skip next section Germany's 1,000th player: 'I had no idea'

Germany's 1,000th player: 'I had no idea'

New Germany international Mika Baur has admitted he was completely unaware that he was making history when he became the 1,000th player to represent the men's national football team.

"I had no idea about it. I found out after the game," the 22-year-old Celtic midfielder said following Germany's 2-0 win over Serbia. "I'm delighted."

Baur came on for goalscorer Tom Bischof in the 77th minute and said the experience was difficult to put into words.

"It's a feeling you have where you hope it doesn't go away," he said.



His phone was flooded with messages when he switched off airplane mode in the dressing room, while his debut shirt is destined for a special place.

"It's going to my parents and will be framed," said Baur, whose father Markus was part of Germany's handball World Cup-winning team in 2007.



Read more about Germany's win over Serbia here: Klopp wins first game as Germany coach, without 'top dogs'

Skip next section German recovery still on shaky ground, trade group warns

German recovery still on shaky ground, trade group warns

Germany's emerging economic recovery remains fragile despite an improving outlook, the country's foreign trade association BGA has warned.

A BGA survey found companies reporting improved business conditions after diversifying supply and distribution routes and adapting to recent crises. However, many firms said red tape was hampering their operations.

"Companies can see light at the end of the tunnel again, but they are still driving with the handbrake on," BGA President Dirk Jandura said.

Leading German economic institutes have raised their growth forecast for this year to 1.3%, up from 0.6% in their spring forecast. The government is also expected to raise its forecast next week.

Debt-financed government spending on infrastructure and defense is a major driver of the expected growth.

Jandura said bureaucracy remained a significant drag, with 82% of companies surveyed naming it as one of the biggest obstacles to competitiveness and 78% saying they had yet to notice any reduction in red tape.

The improvement has also yet to reach the labor market, according to BGA, with more companies in the sector planning to cut jobs than create them.

Skip next section German university graduates rise 3%

German university graduates rise 3%

The number of students and doctoral candidates graduating from German universities has risen by 3%, according to the Federal Statistical Office.

Some 527,600 people completed a degree in 2025, an increase of 16,000 from the previous year. Women accounted for 53% of graduates, unchanged from 2024.

Almost half of all qualifications were bachelor's degrees, with their number rising 4% to 256,000. Master's degrees increased 1% to 150,800.

The number of master's and state-exam qualifications allowing graduates to enter the teaching profession rose 6% to 32,400.

Law, economics and social sciences accounted for the largest share of qualifications at 41%, followed by engineering at 25%.

Skip next section Union slams VW over scrapping labor agreements

Union slams VW over scrapping labor agreements

Germany's IG Metall union has sharply criticized Volkswagen over its latest cost-cutting drive, accusing management of provoking a conflict "that the company cannot afford."

Thorsten Gröger, IG Metall's regional head for Lower Saxony and Saxony-Anhalt, told public broadcaster Deutschlandfunk that VW's approach was "disrespectful toward its own employees" and "irresponsible toward the company itself."

Gröger said worker representatives had listened to a 50-minute presentation from management without hearing "a single word" about plans to terminate key collective bargaining agreements, while the media had already been informed.

He described the move as "unprecedented in the history of Volkswagen" and said employee representatives were prepared for the dispute.

VW says employment conditions need to be revised because of mounting cost pressures.

The carmaker plans to cut 50,000 jobs worldwide in the coming years, on top of previously announced reductions. Around half of the additional cuts could come in Germany.

The longer-term future of entire VW plants in Emden, Hannover and Zwickau, as well as Audi's Neckarsulm site, also remains uncertain.

Skip next section German coalition infighting evokes Scholz-era collapse

German coalition infighting evokes Scholz-era collapse

Germany's conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) is stepping up pressure on its center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) coalition partners ahead of talks next week on a series of contested economic and social reforms.

CDU General Secretary Franziska Hoppermann said Labor Minister Bärbel Bas, who is also an SPD co-leader, needed to produce legislation on pension reform "so that we can finally negotiate concretely."

Her comments to the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (FAZ) newspaper come as Chancellor Friedrich Merz prepares to bring labor market reforms before the coalition committee next week. Merz said this week that Germany had "some catching up to do" when it came to making the labor market more flexible.

The Handelsblatt newspaper reported that CDU parliamentary leaders were considering withholding support for Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil's income tax reform until Bas submits legislation on pensions and the labor market.

One government official described the increasingly fraught atmosphere as "real traffic-light vibes," according to the Handelsblatt, a reference to the bitter disputes that preceded the collapse of former Chancellor Olaf Scholz's three-party "traffic light coalition."

The CDU argues that reforms agreed by the coalition in July were a package and that the SPD cannot expect its preferred measures to go ahead while delaying concessions it made on pensions and the labor market.

Among the most contentious plans is the proposed abolition of penalty-free early retirement after 45 years of contributions. The measure faces opposition within the SPD as well as from several CDU state premiers.

The coalition committee is due to meet next week as the government tries to resolve disputes not only over pensions and the labor market but also taxation, care funding and other reforms.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Tag from DW's newsroom in Bonn.

Things are getting increasingly tense inside Chancellor Friedrich Merz's coalition.

The conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) is piling pressure on its center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) partners to deliver on pension and labor market reforms agreed earlier this year. And the CDU appears ready to play hardball.



The gloves are also coming off at Volkswagen. Germany's IG Metall union has accused VW management of provoking a conflict "that the company cannot afford."



Stay with us here for these stories and more of what Germany is talking about today.

entries.title: Ukraine: Kyiv bridges shut after fatal Russian drone assault
entries.summary: The latest Russian attacks killed at least one person and severely disrupted traffic in the Ukrainian capital. Several bridges over the Dnipro River connect western and eastern Kyiv.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Ukraine: Kyiv bridges shut after fatal Russian drone assault

October 2, 2026

The latest Russian attacks killed at least one person and severely disrupted traffic in the Ukrainian capital. Several bridges over the Dnipro River connect western and eastern Kyiv.

Several bridges in Kyiv have been closed as the result of new Russian drone attacks which killed one person in the city, the Ukrainian capital's authorities said Friday. 

There are a total of eight bridges that connect Kyiv's western and eastern banks along the Dnipro River.

What do we know about the Russian drone attack on Kyiv?

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the city's Southern Bridge, also known as the Pivdennyi Bridge, was "completely closed" to traffic.

The concrete and steel bridge carries road vehicles and a metro rail line. The Southern Bridge has been hit twice over the two days by Russian drone attacks.

The Paton Bridge was also closed to traffic towards the left bank of the Dnipro River, Klitschko said.

Russia's Ministry of Defense said its drones targeted a bridge over the Dnipro which is used for military purposes. Russia also said it attacked a power station in the surrounding Kyiv region alongside the Port of Izmail near the Black Sea and a cargo vessel.  

A Russian attack on Kyiv also left one person in dead and at least two others injured after a strike hit a 25-story building in the Darnytskyi district.

Russia has frequently targeted Kyiv with overnight drone attacks in the years since the start of the February 2022 invasion. Ukraine in response has been developing interceptor technology to down those combat drones.  

Ukraine carries out fresh attacks on Russian oil facilities

Meanwhile, the governor of Russia's southern Volgograd region said Ukrainian drone attacks targeted industrial infrastructure. An apartment building was also damaged in the Ukrainian attack, wounding one person.

Authorities in the southern Russian region of Krasnodar said drone debris damaged an "enterprise" in the Black Sea city of Tuapse.

In a post on X, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces carried out attacks over the past 24 hours on oil facilities in the Samara and Volgograd regions.

"Successful operations were carried out in the Black Sea and in the Voronezh, Nizhny Novgorod, Volgograd, Samara and Krasnodar regions, targeting airfields, industrial facilities, oil refineries, a missile and space center, and an ammunition depot belonging to the occupiers," Zelenskyy said.

Ukraine's military has been targeting oil refineries in Russia over the past year in an attempt to cripple the country's energy industry.

Russian President Vladimir Putin said Thursday that Russia has lost 1% of GDP due to the Ukrainian strikes.  

Edited by: Karl Sexton

entries.title: France: 400 schools closed as student protests continue
entries.summary: Police have made around 2,000 arrests and scores of people have been injured as student protests spread across France. Ministers have called for a "day of dialogue" but students have called for further strike action.
entries.content:
October 2, 2026

Police have made around 2,000 arrests and scores of people have been injured as student protests spread across France. Ministers have called for a "day of dialogue" but students have called for further strike action.

Over 400 schools and colleges across France remained closed on Friday as student protests over education-related grievances continued — with some turning violent.

"There are over ⁠400 schools and other educational establishments that I know of that will be closed," confirmed French Education ​Minister Edouard Geffray on broadcaster ​France 2 late on Thursday night.

The protests ​against teacher shortages, dilapidated school buildings and a lack of learning materials erupted at lycées (equivalent to US high schools) in the Paris region last month before spreading across the country this week.

Student protests in France: damage, injuries, arrests

Police have made around 2,000 arrests and scores of people have been injured, including 40 high school principals, according to Geffray.

Fires were started in at least two high schools on Thursday, while teachers were reportedly inadvertently ​splashed with petrol ⁠at a third in the southern city of Marseille, according to officials.

At ​least one car was torched in the eastern city of Strasbourg while riot police clashed with youths in Toulouse in the southwest.

In the southeastern region of Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes, authorities claimed that "at least €25 million" of damage has been done in their jurisdiction alone.

On Friday, more clashes between student protesters and police were reported in cities across the country, including in Loire, where several officers were injured, and in the capital Paris.

But students have also criticized what they see as a heavy-handed police response.

"You don't want to hear our words; you just fire tear gas," one student wrote on a placard outside the Lycée Voltaire in central Paris (see main photo above).

"Protest is a fundamental right," read another sign.

Minister Geffray told broadcasters on Friday morning that "violent individuals" were "infiltrating groups of students" and "taking the movement hostage" and called on parents to prevent their children from joining the protests.

"What matters now is ensuring our children are no longer out on the streets, because they are in danger," he said.

Geffray was planning to meet with student representatives and trade unions on Friday, saying: "Today will be a day of dialogue."

France: government blames far-left LFI

According to Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, French domestic intelligence agencies told a crisis meeting on Thursday that the movement has been initiated by politicians from the left-wing party La France Insoumise (France Unbowed or LFI) – who have denied the allegations.

Veteran LFI leader and 2027 presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon has indeed supported the protests but called on students to use non-violent methods.

"Students, teachers and educational staff are facing the same state of neglect and their positions and claims should be respected," he wrote in a statement earlier this week, calling for "disciplined struggle, no panic, no irritation."

Meanwhile, student union bodies have called for a day of mass protest next Tuesday, October 6, under the slogan: "Police out of schools! No to the repression of student mobilization!"

"The police have no place in front of educational establishments," read a statement. "We support the ongoing mobilization and call for it to be reinforced."

Edited by: Karl Sexton

entries.title: Ethiopia: Who could bring the warring sides to the negotiation table?
entries.summary: Ethiopia might be facing its most complex armed conflict in contemporary times. The fragile 2022 peace deal has collapsed. International mediators have failed. How will the country return to normal?
entries.content:
Ethiopia

Can anyone broker a new peace between Tigray and Ethiopia?

October 2, 2026

Ethiopia might be facing its most complex armed conflict in contemporary times. The fragile 2022 peace deal has collapsed. International mediators have failed. How will the country return to normal?

Just four years after a landmark peace deal officially halted the devastating Tigray war, fighting has escalated once again in northern Ethiopia in recent weeks. 

Just days before full-scale fighting resumed, several armed groups which had previously considered each enemies formally announced an alliance with a common goal: To bring down Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's federal government.

But this time, the situation looks quite different from the previous conflict: Parties outside the country have been accused of meddling in the situation, with each having their own motives to want to destabilize Abiy's government.

This has raised fears about prolonged instability hitting the Horn of Africa.

Reasons for the collapse of the peace deal

The 2022 Pretoria Peace Agreement ended the conflict between the Ethiopian federal government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which cost hundreds of thousands of lives in the course of two years.

Negash Mohammed, a journalist with DW's Amharic department. believes that the deal collapsed for three key reasons — or rather because three key actors in the conflict were largely neglected at the negotiation table.

The final agreement didn't factor in the role of Eritrea in the conflict, which had fought alongside Ethiopia against the TPLF, Mohammed said. It also ignored the part that Amhara militias — known as Fano — played in the war, who later felt sorely excluded from the negotiations; finally, it ignored hardliners within the TPLF who viewed the peace as a military defeat.

Tensions between the federal government and the Fano escalated further when Abiy's government moved to forcibly disarm the militias instead of addressing their grievances.

"The federal government has its own shortcomings," said Mohammed. "Instead of convincing the other side, it went on to aggravate the grievances they [already] had."

An alliance of former enemies

Mohammed also emphasized that the coalition against the federal government includes several groups which have otherwise little to do with each other.

It includes the Oromo Liberation Army, a faction of the Ogaden National Liberation Front, as well as multiple smaller armed groups from the western Benishangul-Gumuz region and also ethnic militant factions from Afar, which borders Tigray.

Eritrea meanwhile appears to have shifted sides in the current situation: While not officially a member of the alliance, the neighboring country is believed to be providing support to the rebels.

Patricia Rodrigues, a senior analyst at Control Risks, a global intelligence and security consultancy, referred to the level of strategic coordination among these various groups in the current conflict as "quite significant" and "definitely alarming for the federal government."

She noted, however, that cracks might eventually appear: "How long this coalition lasts, because all of them have very different interests and represent very different ethnic constituencies, remains to be seen," she told DW.

Rodrigues added that, based on Control Risks' assessment, the fighting is likely to remain limited to Ethiopia's northern regions, particularly those situated along the borders between Tigray, Amhara and Afar.

Furthermore, she highlighted that the idea of it spreading across the entire country was rather unlikely due to the difficulty of nationwide coordination, taking into consideration the rough terrain of the nation and the fragmentation of other opposition groups.

Could the conflict have been prevented?

Rodrigues also pointed to the failure of sustained international engagement after the end of the crisis in 2022 as a key reason for the current conflict.

She noted that while the Pretoria agreement saw some early proof of implementation — including the TPLF's surrender of heavy weaponry in 2022 and 2023 — international attention had soon shifted to other global crises, leaving both sides free to quietly rearm and conscript supporters.

"It was more of a stopgap or a ceasefire, but people were quickly rearming in the background," she told DW.

The United States had recently lifted sanctions imposed during the 2020–2022 conflict — a step which, according to Mohammed, diminishes the West's leverage in the conflict to push combatants to the negotiating table.

The real cost of war

In the meantime, civilians are bearing the cost of the warring parties: People caught up in the crossfire have been fleeing the conflict once more, adding further to a population of internally displaced persons (IDPs) that has not recovered from the previous war.

"Since 2020, they have not returned to their areas. They are still in makeshift IDP centers," Mohammed said, adding that there have also been isolated reports of drone strikes hitting civilian areas and of rebel groups deploying military hardware inside schools and clinics.

Telephone and internet connections have also been cut in parts of Tigray and Amhara, electricity has been disrupted, and flights have been suspended to several cities including Kombolcha and Lalibela.

Despite official assurances from all parties that civilians would be protected, Mohammed says that the reality on the ground tells a different story: "Words and practice are very contradictory."

Limited prospects for mediation

UN Secretary-General António Guterres dispatched a special envoy to the Horn of Africa, charged with mediating between the African Union, regional powers and Egypt. These are many of the same parties involved in brokering the Pretoria agreement.

But, according to Mohammed, meaningful negotiations are unlikely to bear fruit until at least one of the sides involved in the conflict "comes to understand that this violence will not help them to achieve what they want."

Rodrigues has a similar opinion, stressing that she cannot be optimistic about "an international or a regional mediation being the solution to the current fighting," adding that "intense, but geographically contained" fighting will continue for the foreseeable future.

Adapted from the AfricaLink Podcast by Silja Fröhlich

Edited by: Sertan Sanderson

entries.title: Taiwan: first new F-16V fighters arrive amid China threat
entries.summary: The US-made jets, part of an order made in 2019, touched down as concerns grow in Taiwan that support from the United States could be wavering. Washington insists its policy towards Taiwan and China hasn't changed.
entries.content:
Taiwan

Taiwan: first new F-16V fighters arrive amid China threat

October 2, 2026

The US-made jets, part of an order made in 2019, touched down as concerns grow in Taiwan that support from the United States could be wavering. Washington insists its policy towards Taiwan and China hasn't changed.

Two new F-16V Block 70 fighter jets landed in Taiwan on Friday, the first of a batch of 66 US-made planes ordered back in 2019 as the island nation looks to bolster its defenses in the face of threats posed by neighboring China.

The aircraft, which flew via Hawaii and Guam, touched down at Chihhang Air Base near Taitung on Taiwan's mountainous east coast at midday local time (0400 GMT).

The arrival of the fighter jets was delayed by several months due to reported software issues, and Taiwanese Defense Minister Wellington Koo said more were on the way.

"Of course we won't only have delivered these two by year-end," he told reporters in the capital, Taipei, without providing further details.

"At present, I think aircraft are gradually moving through the production line, and there are also aircraft that have passed tests," he said.

Taiwan fears drop in US support

The delivery comes amid growing concern in Taiwan regarding the United States' commitment to arming Taiwan – and ​a week after US President Donald Trump hosted Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington.

The US insists that there has been no change in policy towards China and Taiwan but Trump has stalled signing off on a new $14 billion package for Taipei. In May, he called it a "very good negotiating chip" in dealings with Beijing, raising fears that Taiwan's security could be traded away.

"We continue standing with friends and allies across the Indo-Pacific to advance our shared prosperity, security, and values — that includes Taiwan," said a US State Department spokesperson when asked about the new F-16Vs.

The jets, made by US defense contractor Lockheed Martin as part of an $8 billion sale agreed seven years ago, are equipped with advanced avionics, and radar systems to better counter the Chinese air force, including its stealthy J-20 fighters — but Washington has been unwilling to provide its most advanced fighters like the F-22 or F-35.

The Taiwanese air force, which scrambles on an almost daily basis in response to aggressive Chinese maneuvers, is expected to have over 200 F-16Vs once deliveries are completed.

"China's intention to annex Taiwan by force has never changed," said Defense Minister ​Koo, referring to Beijing's claims that the democratically governed island belongs to China.

The Chinese foreign ministry has not commented on the arrival of the F-16s but US officials told the Reuters news agency that a Chinese invasion before 2028 is considered increasingly ​unlikely in Washington.

Taiwan: locals welcome arrival of F-16Vs

That assessment didn't stop dozens of locals – some equipped with binoculars and long-lensed cameras – gathering near the air base's perimeter fence to watch the highly anticipated arrival of the jets.

"The threat from the CCP has always been there so we definitely need to strengthen our defense capabilities," Eric Chan, a 57-year-old former air force servicemen, told the AFP news agency, referring to the Chinese Communist Party and stating that the F-16Vs will "play a very important defensive role."

"In terms of hardware capabilities, there will definitely be an improvement," added Kimi Chi, a 37-year-old salesman from the central city of Taichung who had travelled through the night to be able to photograph the aircraft.

"But what we are actually lacking the most right now is pilots. Of course, I hope the government can provide better additional allowances for these military pilots."

Edited by: Karl Sexton

entries.title: India news: Delhi protesters turn up heat on election chief, police tightens security
entries.summary: Hundreds have gathered in central Delhi to demand the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, over the deletion of voters from electoral rolls. Follow DW.
entries.content:
India

India news: Delhi protesters turn up heat on election chief

Published October 2, 2026last updated October 2, 2026

Hundreds have gathered in central Delhi to demand the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, over the deletion of voters from electoral rolls. Follow DW.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Protesters are gathering in New Delhi's Jantar Mantar to demand the election commission chief's resignation
  • They are calling for Gyanesh Kumar to step down amid allegations that voter rolls have been manipulated
  • Police tighten security, saying permission to hold the protest had not been granted

Here are the top headlines from India on Friday, October 2: 

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Police detain over 700 protesters in Delhi

Police detain over 700 protesters in Delhi

Delhi Police on Friday detained more than 700 people, including opposition leaders and members of student organizations, News agency PTI reported in and around the grounds of Jantar Mantar, amid a protest against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

Activists, opposition leaders and student bodies are demanding Kumar's resignation over alleged irregularities in the controversial revision of electoral rolls, which led to mass deletion of voters.

The detentions were made under prohibitory orders issued earlier on Friday to prevent people from assembling, chanting, demonstrating, or giving speeches.

Authorities had earlier clarified that they had not granted protesters permission to demonstrate in central Delhi.

Skip next section In other news from India

In other news from India

PM Modi speaks with Flydubai captain Smit Machchhar

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Friday spoke with Flydubai Captain Smit Machchhar, who was injured in an alleged mid-air attack on a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv, lauding him for his bravery and presence of mind. 

A video of the conversation, posted on the PM's social media, showed the bandaged captain briefing Modi about the incident and about what gave him the courage to confront the attacking co-pilot.

"I was trying to save my own life, but I knew I could not let all those people die," Machchhar said during a call from his hospital bed.

India trade minister meets counterparts on sidelines of G20 event

India's commerce minister Piyush Goyal met with his counterparts from France, Canada, Saudi Arabia and South Korea to discuss furthering bilateral trade, at a time when India is looking to diversify away from the United States. 

The meetings were held on the sidelines of the G20 Trade Ministers' Meeting in Milwaukee.

At the same G20 event, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said he did not think there was "something imminent" on the trade deal with India, News agency PTI reported.

A pending trade deal between New Delhi and Washington has been in a stalemate over threat of new tariffs, sunset clauses and possiblyIndia's use of Russian oil. Greer and Goyal met on Wednesday and said they had a "productive discussion" on the conclusion of an interim trade agreement.

British activist released from Delhi after 9 years in prison

British-Sikh activist Jagtar Singh Johal was released from a prison in Delhi on Thursday after the Indian high court warned the government it would be found in contempt of court. Johal had been in jail for nine years without trial.

The court had ordered Johal's release on September 18 and later warned the government against continued attempts to keep him imprisoned.

Johal was detained on charges of terrorism and targeted killings, and has been a point of diplomatic tensions between India and the UK. While he was acquitted of one terrorism-linked charge in March 2025, eight other charges remain.

Skip next section Election body orders 'special drive' to enroll 'left out' voters

Election body orders 'special drive' to enroll 'left out' voters

The Election Commission of India has directed 20 of India's states and union territories to conduct a "special drive" to enroll voters who were "left out" during the controversial revision of electoral rolls. The ECI posted the order, dated October 1, on X on Friday.

"Voter enrollment is a continuous process and any person not yet enrolled in the electoral roll or whose name has got deleted can apply for enrollment at any point of time. The objective of the special drive is to identify and facilitate such electors," the order said.

This comes amid increasing scrutiny of the controversial revision of polling lists and protests in central Delhi over the scale of voters deleted from electoral rolls.

Skip next section Police deploys water cannons, tear gas at protest site

Police deploys water cannons, tear gas at protest site

Protesters began arriving near the heavily barricaded grounds of Jantar Mantar in central Delhi early on Friday morning. DW reporters on the ground witnessed police detaining people, seemingly at random.

Around 11:15 a.m. local time (0545 GMT), a large rally led by the Students' Federation of India (SFI) reached the site. The SFI is a leftist students' body, which, along with others, has been demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's ouster.

Protesters clashed with the police as authorities tried to block the road leading to Jantar Mantar.

Water cannons and tear-gas shell launchers were deployed at the scene, although they have not yet been used.

Skip next section How does this related to Narendra Modi's BJP?

How does this related to Narendra Modi's BJP?

The protests against CEC Gyanesh Kumar are partially being viewed as renewed pressure on Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government.

The reason behind it may not be immediately obvious since the Election Commission of India (ECI) is meant to be an independent body. But this might help:

Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, along with Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, comprise the Election Commission of India.

They are responsible for overseeing elections and related projects such as the SIR exercise, which is meant to remove redundancies in India's electoral rolls.

Opposition leaders and critics have argued that those struck off in the exercise include a heavy proportion of minority voters and that Prime Minister Narendra Modi's BJP is using it as a tool to secure future electoral wins. They have also accused ECI chief Kumar of doing the central government's bidding even though the institute is meant to maintain its independence.

The BJP has dismissed those claims, arguing that those removed largely involve dead voters and illegal infiltrators, thereby protecting India's democracy.

Moreover, a 2023 law introduced by the Modi government changed the way the ECI Chief was appointed, giving the government a greater say. Critics have questioned Kumar's credibility and ability to stay independent given the government's heavy role in his appointment.

Skip next section Why are people protesting?

Why are people protesting?

Pressure on Kumar intensified in September after the Indian Express newspaper reported that two of the three election commissioners had formally raised concerns over aspects of the Special Intensive Revisions (SIR) at least 14 times over the past 10 months.

The objections relate to new voter registrations, deletion and restoration of voters in the rolls, filing of appeals against orders restoring voters in the SIR process and the custody and security of the entire electoral roll itself, the report said.

In one of the objections, Sandhu complained that the Election Commission acted against the written advice of two commissioners and claimed its action was "unauthorized and illegal."

The Election Commission had dismissed concerns of an internal rift, saying differing views were a "normal" part of deliberations and that all its actions were lawful.

Over 130 million Indian voters have been struck off the draft voters list across 30 states and union territories, the Indian Express report said, putting the ECI in the middle of a national debate over who votes and who doesn't.

Skip next section Protesters gather in Jantar Mantar to demand Gyanesh Kumar's resignation amid heavy security

Protesters gather in Jantar Mantar to demand Gyanesh Kumar's resignation amid heavy security

Thousands of protesters, activists, opposition members and student bodies are expected to gather in central Delhi's iconic Jantar Mantar grounds today to demand the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

The protest is the latest escalation in growing scrutiny of the poll-governing body of the largest democracy in the world — long regarded as one of the country's most trusted independent institutions.

Political pressure group Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) will not be demonstrating in New Delhi today, according to a clarification posted on X earlier this week.

The group is, however, scheduled to hold a rally against Kumar in Mumbai on Friday, and plans to take the demonstrations nationwide in the coming days.

Visuals coming out of central Delhi showed heavy police and security deployment. Several entry points to the grounds have been barricaded, and authorities have imposed a prohibitory order under Indian law, according to news agency ANI.

Under this order, public meetings, assemblies of five or more people, processions, sloganeering, demonstrations and making speeches without permission are prohibited.

Incidentally, today is the birth anniversary of Mahatma Gandhi, informally known as the "father of the nation." Gandhi is known for his non violent demonstrations, marches and hunger strikes, contributing to British India's freedom movement against colonial rule and ultimately leading to India's independence in 1947.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage!

Welcome to our coverage!

Hello, and welcome to DW's India blog!

This is Mahima from Studio Delhi, where the thermometer is beginning to dip with every passing day.

But the heat is still on in the national capital, with protesters gathering at the iconic Jantar Mantar grounds in central Delhi. These are the same grounds which acted as the base for the Cockroach movement a few months ago, leading to the ouster of India's then education minister. 

Now, the Chief of India's Election Commission is under fire with protesters demanding his resignation over his role in a controversial revision of electoral rolls which reportedly led to deletion of over 130 million voters across 30 states and union territories. 

Authorities have beefed up security in the area, and several metro stations have been shut to limit public access.

DW has multiple reporters on the ground to bring you the latest.

Stay tuned!
